full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This Rule Nisi under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned criminal proceedings being BACGR. Case No. 9 of 2002 arising out of Sabujbag PS. Case No. 27 dated 16-1-2002 pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate so far as it relates to the petitioner should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and why the respondents should not be directed to refrain from taking any action or passing any order against the petitioner or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 4. The Assistant Commissioner of Customs on receiving the same passed an order on the same date in the body of the said letter directing the Superintendent-I, entry section, not to release the consignment without having prior "no objection certificate" from the Bond Commissionerate. The Commissioner of Customs by a forwarding letter dated 11-7-2001 (Annexure-G) sent a copy of the letter (Annexure-G) to the petitioner which the petitioner received on 15-7-2001 and on the same day, the petitioner asked the Assistant Commissioner to ensure compliance of the direction. Before receiving instruction from the Commissioner of Customs, vide Annexure-G1, the petitioner started taking precautionary measure on his own on the basis of the letter of respondent No. 5 dated 24-6-2001. In the process of taking step in the matter, the petitioner wrote a letter to respondent No.5 on 27-6-2001 informing him that container under rotation number 737 of 2001 had arrived ICD Kamlapur. In the said letter, it was also mentioned that no bill of entry had been submitted against the consignment and that if bill of entry had been submitted, the consignment could not have been released without obtaining "no objection" from respondent No.5. It was further stated that on receipt of the instruction of the Commissioner of Customs on 15-7-2001, the petitioner instructed the Assistant Commissioner, ho was in charge of assessment and examination of imported and exportable goods, for ensuring necessary action in accordance with the letter of respondent No.5 dated 24-6-2001 Annexure-G2). Thereafter, on the instruction of the petitioner, a copy of the letter (Annexure-G2) was sent to the Superintendent (Import-Examination) for necessary action because he was responsible for actual delivery of the goods after payment of duty and issuance of out pass. Mr Shajahan, working for port Authority in ICD Kamlapur, received the said letter on 10-7-2001. As per section 12 of the Chittagong Port Authority Ordinance, 1976 the port authority is the custodian of the imported goods and after arrival, the goods are to be released from the port as and when the out pass is issued by the Customs Authority after payment of duties and charges by the importer. In the letter dated 24-6-2001 (Annexure-G) issued by respondent No.5, the importer of consignment under rotation No. 737 of 2001 was mentioned as Cargo Movers/Honorway Textile and Apparels (Pvt.) Ltd. Since the owner of one of the consignments in question was mentioned as Honor way which submitted 8 bills of entries on 28- 6-2001 for the purpose of clearing 8 other consignments, a letter was issued under the signature of the Superintendent on behalf of the petitioner on 2-7-2001 to respondent No. 5 requesting him to inform as to whether or not respondent No.5 had got any objection in releasing the goods imported by Honor way. Although the said 8 other consignments were not mentioned in the letter dated 24-6-2001 of respondent No.5, the petitioner being more vigilant and concerned about protecting Government revenue caused the issuance of the said letter dated 2-7-2001 (Annexure-H) as the importer was the same person. In the meantime, Honor way Textile and Apparels (Pvt.) Ltd. wrote a letter on 4-7-2001 (Annexure-I) informing him that consignment under rotation No. 737 of 2001 was not owned by them and they had not imported the same. By letter dated 4-7-2001 (Annexure-I-I), respondent No.5 informed the petitioner that, since the imported containers were not mentioned in the letter dated 24-6-2001, they got nothing to do with those 8 consignments. The goods under the above rotation arrived on 22-6-2001 and as per section 82 of the Customs Act, 1969, the goods in question were to be kept at the port area upto 45 days and within that period the petitioner had no authority to take any action in respect of the goods. Moreover, in the letter dated 24-6-2001, respondent No. 5 mentioned Cargo Movers/Honorway as the owner of the consignment under rotation 737 of 2001. Of the two owners, one of them denied ownership in respect of the aforesaid consignment but the other alleged owner i.e., the first owner, Cargo Movers, as mentioned by respondent No. 5 in the letter dated 24-6-2001, did not deny the ownership. On 24-7- 2001, the petitioner came to learn from Mr Kazi Harunoor Rashid, Customs Inspector, who was on duty at the delivery gate on the night of 23-7-2001, that some unknown persons took out the consignment referred to in Annexure-'G' (hereinafter mentioned as disputed consignment) from the ICD port protected area, Kamlapur. Hearing the news of the same, the petitioner rushed to his office and enquired about the incident. After taking stock of the whole situation, the petitioner informed the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Dhaka about the whole situation in writing, vide letter dated 24-7-2001 (Annexure-J) proposing action against the persons who were responsible for violation of the direction repeatedly given. A copy of the said letter was also sent to respondent No.5 for information. Immediately after the incident the petitioner sent one of his Inspectors to the Sabujbag Police Station to ledge a GD entry about the incident but the police instead of lodging the GD entry informed the Inspector that on the selfsame incident a regular case was started on the basis of the information received from the Port Authority. On the basis of the letter dated 24-7-2001 of the petitioner, the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Dhaka served a notice for showing cause upon the port authority. Respondent No.6 issued a notice upon the petitioner through the Commissioner of Customs, Customs House, Dhaka asking him to file representation within 7 days as regards his responsibility and accountability in the matter (Annexure-12). The petitioner replied to the said notice by elaborating in minute details about the incident as evident from (Annexure-K). Thereafter, the Secretary, Ministry of Finance in the Internal Resource Division constituted an inter-ministerial enquiry committee consisting of 4 members to hold an enquiry into the matter and to submit report within one month. Among the members of the committee one was respondent No. 5 who was directly or indirectly involved in the matter in dispute. The Committee submitted the report within one week. The petitioner was served with a notice for showing cause on 4-10-2001. On receiving the said notice, the petitioner filed an application before the authority to supply a copy of the report of the enquiry which was accordingly given to him. The petitioner replied to the said police by elaborating in minute details about the incident, steps taken by him and his subordinate and action taken as evident from Annexure-L. Thereafter, the petitioner received charge-sheet along with statement of allegations under memo dated 9-12-2001. (Annexure-L1 ). The petitioner replied. to the said notice as evident from (Annexure-M). In the meantime, respondent No.4 issued a notice upon the petitioner asking him to appear before him for the purpose of conducting an enquiry into the allegations of taking away of the consignment in question (Annexure-M1 ). Suddenly, the petitioner came to know that a case was started against him being BACGR. Case No. 9 of 2002 corresponding to Sabujbag Police Station Case No. 27 dated 16-1-2002, on the selfsame allegations for which a departmental proceeding had already been started. The petitioner had in the facts aforestated no criminal involvement or any malfeasance in the matter and he having performed his duty, the present proceeding is harming his reputation as a citizen and as a servant of the Republic. 

 6. Respondent No. 3 filed an affidavit-in-opposition controverting the statements made in the Writ petition. The case of respondent No.3, in short, is that the paper works done by the petitioner was nothing but a show of business. This was proved by the 4-member departmental enquiry committee which found that the petitioner was liable for the missing containers as per provisions of sections 17 and 168 of the Customs Act, 1969. The petitioner could have seized the alleged consignment but instead of doing so, he made a scope for taking the, container out of ICD boundary. The unclaimed consignment had been taken out of the ICD boundary in connivance with the petitioner and others. The Anti-Corruption officials had found alleged involvement of the petitioner having considered circumstantial perspective along with papers, and subsequently, lodged first information report with the concerned Police Station. For the reasons stated, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 7. Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the petitioner having performed his duty in issuing necessary order for preventing release of the disputed consignment which was released by fraud and forgery by others, particularly by those under whose custody the consignment was, the impugned proceeding being BACGR. Case No. 9 of 2002 before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka is without any factual basis and without lawful authority so far as it relates to the petitioner. He further submits that at any rate, the consignment was in the custody of the port authority, and that its employees released the consignment without the requisite documents from Customs authority, particularly without any authority from the petitioner and so, the petitioner cannot be made liable for the infraction of the port employees. He also submits that except for an omnibus statement, there is no statement, which can even remotely connect the petitioner with the crime and, as such, the proceeding so far as it relates to the petitioner is without lawful authority and cannot be continued. He lastly submits that the 3-member enquiry, committee constituted by the Government found that the petitioner performed his duties properly and that relying on the report of the enquiry the Government exonerated the petitioner from the charges levelled against him in the departmental proceeding and, as such, the impugned proceeding so far as it relates to the petitioner is liable to be quashed 

 "82. Procedure in case of goods-not cleared or warehoused or transhipped after unloading within a specified period-(1) If any goods are not entered and cleared for home consumption or warehoused or transhipped within forty-five days of the date of unloading thereof at a customs port or a land customs station, or within thirty days of the date of unloading thereof at a customs airport, or within such extended period as the appropriate officer may allow, such goods may, after due notice given to the owner, if his address could be ascertained, or published in the newspaper, if his address could not be ascertained, be sold under the orders of the appropriate officer: 

 15. The fate of this Rule Nisi hinges on its maintainability. In this regard, Mr Mahmudul Islam cited a number of cases. In the case of State of Haryana and others vs Ch. Bhajan Lal and others, AIR 1992 (SC) 604, an first information report was lodged under sections 161 and 165 of the Indian Penal Code and under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Supreme Court of India, in the case referred to above, held as follows: "In the backdrop of the interpretation of the various relevant provisions of the Code under Chapter XIV and of the principles of, law enunciated by this Court in a series of decisions relating to the exercise of the extraordinary power under Article 226 or the inherent powers under section 482 of the Code which we have extracted and reproduced' above we give the following categories of cases by way of illustration wherein such power could be exercised either to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice, though it may not be possible to lay down any precise, clearly defined and sufficiently channelised and inflexible guidelines or rigid formulae and to give an exhaustive list of myriad kinds of cases wherein such power should be exercised. 

 1. Where the allegations made in the First Information Report or the complaint, even if they are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety do not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused. 

 3. Where the uncontroverted allegations made in the first information report or complaint and the evidence collected in support of the same do not disclose the commission of any offence and make out a case against the accused. 

 16. The Supreme Court of India, however, found that such power should be exercised sparingly and that too in the rarest of rare cases. The judgment spelt out as many as seven grounds calling for quashment of a criminal case under the writ jurisdiction. From the judgment referred to above, it does not, however, appear that before moving the application under Articles 226 and 227 of the Indian Constitution, the accused surrendered before the Court of Magistrate. 

 17. In the case of Messrs Pepsi Foods Ltd and another vs Special Judicial Magistrate and others, AIR 1998 (SC) 128, it was held as follows: 

 "It is no comfortable thought for the appellants to be told that they could appear before the Court which is at a far off place in Ghazipur in the State of Uttar Pradesh, seek their release on bail and then to either move an application under section 245(2) of the Code or to face trial when the complaint and the preliminary evidence recorded makes out no case against them. It is certainly one of those cases where there is an abuse of the process of the law and the Courts and the High Court should not have shied away in exercising its jurisdiction. Provisions of Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution and section 482 of the Code are devised to advance justice and not to frustrate it. In our view the High Court should not have adopted such a rigid approach which certainly has led to miscarriage of justice in the case. Power of judicial review is discretionary but this was a case where the High Court should have exercised it. 

 18. From the above case, it appears that the provisions of Articles 226 and 227 can be resorted to for quashment of a criminal case to prevent abuse of the process of law and of the Court and that the High Court should not have shied away in exercising its jurisdiction. 

 19. In the case of State of West Bengal and others vs Swapan Kumar Guha and Others, AIR 1982 (SC) 949, the Supreme Court of India approved the judgment delivered by the Calcutta High Court which made the Rule absolute on an application filed under Article 226 of the Indian: Constitution, and held as follows: 

 20. From the cases referred to above, it appears that 1 in special circumstances the writ jurisdiction is attracted for quashing a criminal proceeding. Exercise of such power would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case but with the sole purpose to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. 

 21. In the case of Saidur Rahman alias Chan Miah and others vs State 40 DLR (AD) 281, the Sessions Judge found the appellants guilty of charge under section 147 of the Penal Code and granted interim bail pending filing of appeal. The High Court Division summarily dismissed the appeal holding that the appellants were fugitives from law as they did not surrender before moving their application of appeal. The Appellate Division held that in the facts and circumstances of the case, it would be less than charitable to attribute to the appellants that they were fugitives from justice and that there was nothing in their conduct to show that they were running away from the jurisdiction of the Court or avoiding its process. 

 22. In the case in hand, just an first information report was filed and warrant of arrest was yet to be issued by the Magistrate. By filing the Writ Petition, the petitioner has been before this Court and therefore, he cannot be termed a fugitive from justice. Moreover, we have already referred to a case reported in AIR 1998 (SC) 128 in which the accused filed a Writ petition notwithstanding the fact that they did not surrender before the Court of Magistrate. The Supreme Court of India even then found that the Writ petition was maintainable, set aside the judgment passed by the High Court and quashed the complaint and proceeding against the appellants. 

 23. The learned Additional Attorney-General, however, contends that the petitioner's remedy lies under section 561-A of the CrPC. Contradicting his contention, Mr Mahmudul Islam submits that in an application filed under section 561 A, CrPC, the defence case cannot be pleaded and therefore, the petitioner was compelled to invoke the writ jurisdiction of this Court. 

 "A question has arisen as to the status of an accused Government servant against whom a warrant of arrest is issued but he absconds to avoid arrest, subsequently surrenders before the Court, and thereafter is granted bail by the Court. The matter has been examined by the Government. The legal position is that when an accused Government Servant surrenders before the Court and is thereafter granted bail by the Court, he shall be deemed to have been taken into custody and should be considered as under suspension as per Notes 1 and 2 under rule 73 of the BSR, Part 1. Similarly, in any other cases of release on bail also, the Government Servant concerned should be considered as under suspension within the meaning of Note 2 under the said rule 73". 

 27. The aforesaid findings arrived at by us are, however, not sufficient to exonerate the petitioner from the accusation made against him in the first information report by the Bureau of Anti-Corruption. We are of the view that if a criminal proceeding is quashed in Writ jurisdiction, such a precedent will open a floodgate and the litigants instead of appearing before the Criminal Courts will directly come before this Court by invoking its Writ jurisdiction. We, however, find that the case in hand is the rarest of rare cases in which the Writ jurisdiction can reasonably be invoked. The special feature of this case is that the Ministry of Finance, Internal Resources Division, constituted a high- powered committee consisting of three high officials who in their report (Annexure-S) found that the petitioner had performed his duty in respect of the consignment under rotation number 737 of 2001 in accordance with law. On the basis of that report the Ministry, that is, the Government, exonerated the petitioner from the departmental proceeding. The Government, however, has allowed a criminal case to proceed against the petitioner on the self-same occurrence. Such an attitude of the Government in two different forums cannot be accepted. Since the Government exonerated the petitioner from the departmental proceeding, we find that the criminal proceeding so far as it relates to the petitioner should be quashed in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. 

 29. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute and the impugned proceeding of BACGR Case No.9 of 2002 arising out of Sabujbag PS Case No. 27 dated 16-1-2002 pending before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka is quashed so far as it relates to the petitioner. The criminal case will, however, proceed against the other accused. There is no order as to costs.
